question.text: Can mass drug administration lead to the sustainable control of schistosomiasis?
question.context: In the Philippines, the current national control strategy for schistosomiasis is annual mass drug administration (MDA) with 40 mg/kg of praziquantel in all schistosomiasis-endemic villages with a prevalence ≥10%. A cross-sectional survey of schistosomiasis was conducted in 2012 on 18 221 individuals residing in 22 schistosomiasis-endemic villages in the province of Northern Samar. The prevalence of schistosomiasis, intensity of Schistosoma infection, and morbidity of disease were assessed. Despite an active schistosomiasis-control program in Northern Samar for>30 years, which included a MDA campaign in the last 5 years, the mean prevalence of schistosomiasis among 10 435 evaluated subjects was 27.1% (95% confidence interval [CI], 26.3%-28.0%), and the geometric mean intensity of infection among 2832 evaluated subjects was 17.2 eggs per gram of feces (95% CI, 16.4-18.1). Ultrasonography revealed high levels of schistosomiasis-induced morbidity in the schistosomiasis-endemic communities. Left lobe liver enlargement (≥70 mm) was evident in 89.3% of subjects. Twenty-five percent of the study population had grade II/III liver parenchyma fibrosis, and 13.3% had splenomegaly (≥100 mm).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The clinical case describes a schistosomiasis-endemic area with a high prevalence (27.1%) and intensity of infection (17.2 eggs/g feces) despite a long-standing control program including MDA. The high prevalence and morbidity (liver enlargement, fibrosis, splenomegaly) suggest that MDA alone is insufficient to achieve sustainable control. Therefore, mass drug administration is unlikely to lead to sustainable control.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The high prevalence of schistosomiasis (27.1%) and the presence of significant morbidity (liver enlargement, fibrosis, splenomegaly) despite a long-standing MDA program indicate that MDA alone is not sufficient to achieve sustainable control.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Other potential causes of liver enlargement and fibrosis were considered, but the context of a known schistosomiasis-endemic area and the presence of eggs in stool strongly points towards schistosomiasis as the primary driver of the observed findings. Other conditions like viral hepatitis or autoimmune liver diseases were less likely given the prevalence of schistosomiasis in the community.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The high prevalence (27.1%) and intense infection (17.2 eggs/g) despite a long-standing MDA program indicate that current strategies are insufficient. The presence of significant morbidity (liver enlargement, fibrosis) suggests ongoing disease burden. Annual MDA alone has not reduced transmission enough to achieve sustainable control, as evidenced by persistent high infection levels and organ damage.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The 27.1% prevalence and 17.2 eggs/g intensity show that MDA is not effectively reducing transmission or infection intensity in Northern Samar.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Environmental control measures (e.g., snail control) were not mentioned in the data, but the persistent high burden suggests they may be inadequate. The focus on MDA alone without snail control is likely a key limitation.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: Despite decades of MDA with praziquantel, the 2012 survey showed persistent high prevalence (27.1%) and intensity (17.2 eggs/g) of infection, along with severe morbidity (e.g., 89.3% liver enlargement, 25% fibrosis). This indicates MDA alone is insufficient for sustainable control without additional interventions such as snail control or improved sanitation.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Mean prevalence of 27.1% and high morbidity rates (89.3% liver enlargement, 25% fibrosis) despite >30 years of MDA indicate failure of sustainable control.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Other interventions like snail control or water sanitation were not mentioned as part of the strategy, so their absence was considered a key factor in MDA’s limited success; thus, MDA alone is not sufficient for sustainable control.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Mass drug administration is effective for reducing transmission but not for eliminating infection or stopping all disease-related complications in endemic communities; other interventions such as health education, treatment of active cases, and improved sanitation would be needed for true sustainability.
